title: About Sydney Martin
text:
By: Sydney Martin




About the Creator
My name is Sydney Martin, and I am a student-athlete at New College of Florida in Sarasota, Florida, originally from North Carolina. Having competed in wrestling since my freshman year of high school, I currently represent New College on the women’s wrestling team.
I created this project to share the importance of collegiate women’s wrestling and to inform people about this rapidly growing sport to expand public knowledge and showcase its unprecedented rise.
As female student-athletes continue to break barriers and push the boundaries of collegiate combat sports, having accessible data, comprehensive tournament archives, and clear visibility is essential to honoring their achievements and inspiring the next generation.


Why This Project Matters

Sharing the Importance: Highlighting the dedication, grit, and athletic excellence of female wrestlers competing at the highest collegiate levels.
Informing & Expanding Knowledge: Providing an accessible, searchable archive covering 3,100+ bouts, team legacies, All-American placers, and rosters.
Showcasing Explosive Growth: Documenting how NAIA women’s wrestling pioneered collegiate combat sports by becoming the first association to grant full championship status.

Note📋 Note on 2023 Tournament Data



Official match-by-match bout logs and participant counts for the 2023 National Championship were not available in the public tournament archives, so 2023 numbers are omitted from the timeline (similarly, the 2020 tournament was cancelled nationwide due to COVID-19).










Tip🏫 Why School Numbers Shifted After 2022



Between 2022 and 2024, the tournament transitioned from an open national invitational to an official championship sport. In the open era (2019–2022), any school could enter multiple athletes, leading to an uncapped peak of 40 colleges in 2022. Beginning in 2024, NAIA instituted strict conference qualifying tournaments and capped brackets at 20 wrestlers per weight class, so only the top ~35–36 schools with automatic conference qualifiers advance to nationals.

section: Why This Matters: The Importance & Rapid Growth
text:
Why This Matters: The Importance & Rapid Growth
Women’s wrestling is breaking barriers across collegiate athletics. When the National Association of Intercollegiate Athletics (NAIA) became the first collegiate governing body to grant women’s wrestling full championship sport status, it ignited a nationwide movement:

Empowering Female Athletes: Women’s wrestling requires immense discipline, technical precision, and resilience, providing female student-athletes an elite collegiate arena in one of the world’s most demanding combat sports.
Explosive National Growth: What began in 2019 as a 20-team invitational has rapidly expanded into over 40 varsity programs spanning coast to coast, fielding hundreds of collegiate competitors annually.
Preserving Every Historic Milestone: From the inaugural pins in 2019 to the newest 2026 national champions, this archive preserves the individual legacies and team rivalries driving the sport forward.

title: NAIAWomen’s WrestlingChampionships
text:
Data & Methodology
The data powering this archive was gathered from official championship bout logs and tournament results (2019–2026). Built using R, Quarto, tidyverse, and reactable, this project aims to preserve history and provide an interactive platform that demonstrates the enduring power and growth of collegiate women’s wrestling.
